And one may only declare such a split kosher on the back, where the split rests upon the depression, but on the front the split falls downward and is ultimately destined to be detached and is terefah. Thus far his words. And that which is implied by his wording, that the reason a surplus lobe on the back is terefah is because it is ultimately destined to be detached, is not exact, for it has already been explained that the reason is because "surplus is as if missing." Rather, this is what he is saying: even if we say regarding a surplus lobe on the back that what the sages, of blessed memory, said—that it is terefah—was due to the reason of friction against the ribs, and according to this the law would be the same for a split, to this he says that it is not so, for even according to that reason it is kosher in a split, for it is not destined to be detached because it has a depression in which to rest [so I am compelled to explain, for otherwise he contradicts himself, and examine this closely].

And that which he wrote, "falls into the pit and is level with the rest of the lung," his intention is that it fills the entire pit, to exclude if it protrudes upward; even if it is like a mound that is not sharp, it is terefah. And there is one who says that even if its height is not like a myrtle leaf, since in the entire split there is the size of a myrtle leaf, it is terefah, because there are two defects in this: one, that it was split from the lung, and the second, that the slight protrusion will rub against the ribs. And all the more so if it protrudes because it is wider than the pit and it is impossible for it to reach the bottom of the pit, it is terefah [Siman 38, section 18], not like those who are lenient when the protrusion is less than a myrtle leaf [see Tevuot Shor, subsection 23]. And it is simple that if by means of a strong inflation it is level with the rest of the lung, one should permit it. And if the entire split is less than a myrtle leaf, it is permitted simply, for even if we say that it will rub against the ribs, nevertheless, since an extra lobe on the back is permitted in less than this measure, all the more so a split on the back, even though it does not fill the pit; for anything less than this measure does not have the power to damage, for so did our Sages, of blessed memory, receive. Therefore, it seems to me that in a case of great loss, one should be lenient also when the protrusion is less than a myrtle leaf even if in its totality there is the measure, provided it is clear that this is a split and not an extra lobe, for anything less than the measure one should be lenient in a case of great loss; and it requires further study for the practical law.

And if the split is smaller than the indentation, such that it does not fill the entire indentation, some say it is treifah, for this is a sign that it is not a split but rather an extra lobe. And some say it is kosher, for ultimately, since it rests in an indentation, it is not destined to be separated. And if it is difficult to understand why, if it is a split from the lung, it does not fill the entire indentation, one can say that it has been split for a long time, and the lung grew along with the indentation, while the split, due to its weakness, did not grow as much as the main lung and the indentation. And since there is an indentation beneath it, it is like a clarification that this is a split and not an extra lobe.

The standard split is such that the side connected to it is toward the spine and the side of separation is below, and therefore our teacher, the Rema, ruled it kosher even though it does not enter into the cavity on its own, but rather when one places the hand upon it gently; for just as it enters into the animal with the placement of the hand, so too during its life, when the split reaches the chest wall, it descends into the cavity. But if the side of separation is toward the spine and the connected side is below, it is self-evident that it is not so stationary that it would enter into the cavity. Therefore, there are some of the books of the examiners who wish to be stringent in such a case, but from the silence of the wording of the poskim, it is clear that there is no distinction, for if it were not so, they should have explained this. Therefore, one of the great authorities wrote that in such a case we are not so lenient that the grasp of a human hand should suffice, rather if through inflation it goes on its own into the cavity, one must certainly rule it kosher, for it was certainly resting within the cavity during its life. But if they must place the hand upon it until it enters into the cavity, the experts look and estimate according to the value of the split and its connection; and if according to their estimation it fell into the cavity during its life when it struck the ribs, they rule it kosher, and if not, one should not be lenient [Siman 38, section 19], and these are words of reason.

And this that he rules treif regarding a split from the front, the reason is simple: because it is destined to separate since it is into the cavity. Thus it is found that a split is the exact opposite of an extra lobe, for an extra lobe from the front is kosher according to many poskim and from the back is treif, whereas a split is the opposite, as from the front it is treif and from the back it is kosher due to the reasons that have been explained. And that which we do not fear regarding an extra lobe from the front that perhaps it will separate is because it is rooted well in the manner of the lobes, for the essence of the creation is such; this is not the case with a split that split from the lung, for it has been damaged, and certainly there is a great concern that when it is from the front it will fall into the lung.

And know that there are several of the great authorities who said that even regarding a split from the beginning, if it is rooted well, we do not fear that it might become detached, and it is kosher. And there are those who cried out against this like a crane. And even according to the opinion of those who permit it, we do not know what is called "rooted well." And I saw one who says that if the split goes in a circle, and more than half of the circle is rooted in the lung, such that the hanging side is much less than the rooted side, this is called "rooted well," for it will automatically hold the small hanging part so that it does not become detached. But if the split is like a square—and not specifically a square, but even long and short—yet if the rooted side is not more than the hanging side, it is certainly easy for it to become detached. And it is a correct reasoning, and one whose heart is whole in the matter may be lenient in a case of great loss when it is rooted very well.

If there is a doubt whether this is a split or a redundancy in a manner where it is impossible to distinguish, there is one who says that one should attribute it more likely to a redundancy [B.A.]. I do not know why, for according to what our eyes see, both this and that are not very common. It would have been possible to say that since the majority of animals are kosher and it was slaughtered while standing in its status of permissibility, one should be lenient in this, whether from the front or from the back, and attribute it in every manner to declare it kosher. However, regarding a defect that occurred during life, there is room to doubt whether one may permit it based on this reason, as I wrote in siman 29, and as will be further explained in siman 50. Therefore, the primary rule in this is to gather the slaughterers of the city, and it is inevitable that they will not fail to recognize well whether this is a split or a redundancy.

He further wrote: A lobe that split and has one root the thickness of a finger is considered only as one. Thus far his words. The explanation of these matters is that this is not similar to the split that was explained, for a split is specifically when it does not stand at the slopes but in the body of the lung with a depression beneath it. But anything that is divided into two, whether in length, width, or thickness, is not to be considered a split but a division, as long as the observer sees with his eyes that it resembles the form of a division. Therefore, when they have one root the thickness of a finger, it is considered only as one. And some say that this is to declare it treif, but to declare it kosher, such as where a lobe is missing, it is obvious that it is no worse than the permissibility of a crack that was explained. And consequently, it is only effective in a place where a crack is effective, such as where it is in a place where there is normally a division of lobes. And if they do not have one root, one of them is an extra lobe. And if both of them lie equally, it is an extra lobe in the row of lobes and is kosher. And if one is higher than its fellow, and its fellow is as if it lies beneath it, the experts must identify according to their length, width, and thickness if one is the primary one and its fellow lying beneath it is the extra one—then it is an extra lobe from the front; and if its fellow is the primary one, then the one that is higher is the extra one, and it is an extra lobe on its back. And there is a great principle to know: that any matter that depends on expertise according to the sight of the eyes is impossible to explain entirely in writing, and a teacher has only what his eyes see, in conjunction with the expert shochatim, and with a prayer to Hashem that they should not stumble in a matter of halacha. For this we see with our eyes, that with all the abundance of books from the very latest authorities on the laws of examinations, nevertheless there are new cases every morning that are not explained in the books. Therefore, the sage whose heart is whole and who is expert in lungs—a judge has only what his eyes see.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: The right lobe adjacent to the windpipe in the narrow part of the chest right next to the neck—the lowest one which is the uppermost adjacent to the neck—if there is found upon its back something like a myrtle leaf, it is kosher because it is its nature to split. And specifically the right one, but not the left. And there is one who says that specifically above its half, but below its half it is treifah. Thus far his words. And in his great book he explained that in the rest of the lobes it is treifah, see there. And it must be understood, for we permit a split in all the lobes when it is on its back, and he himself brought this in his great book. And it must be said that this is the explanation: that in the other lobes it is not kosher unless there is a depression beneath it, but without a depression it is an extra growth from its back and is treifah. But in the lobe adjacent to the windpipe it is kosher even without a depression, because due to the pressure of the chest it is its nature to split, and therefore we attribute this to a split and not to an extra growth. And it is not specifically like a myrtle leaf, for the same law applies even to more than a myrtle leaf [acharonim]; rather, he mentioned the measurement of a lobe which is like a myrtle leaf, for in less than this measurement it is kosher in all the lobes and in the entire lung, as has been written. And therefore it is only kosher on the right and not on the left, because on the left there is no pressure of the chest and we do not attribute it to a split. and even though the upper left lobe is also adjacent to the windpipe, nevertheless it is not like the narrow part of the chest.

And that which he wrote, that there is one who says that specifically above its half, but below its half it is terefah, the interpretations of this have multiplied. Some say that both are in the width of the ouna, and "above its half" refers to what is toward the sharp edge, and "below its half" refers to what is toward the root; and according to this, what is toward the sharp edge is kosher throughout the entire length of the ouna. And some say that we even measure by the length of the ouna, meaning that the half-width that we declared kosher is only above its half in its length toward the windpipe, and not the second half which is toward the lung [Taz subsection 8 in the name of the Rashal]. And some say that the groove of the ouna is the boundary of the location, for from the groove toward the sharp edge it is kosher, and from the groove toward the root it is terefah [Shulchan Melachim section 15], and everything outside the groove is terefah in any location. And the reason for all these opinions is according to their estimation of in which location is the primary pressure of the chest. And there is one who wrote that the custom is to measure in this manner: that we take the left ouna and place it against the right, and from the place where the left ouna ends and onward is called "toward the sharp edge," which is toward the head, and it is kosher; and from the place where the left ouna reaches and toward the lung, it is called "below its half" and it is terefah [Be'er Heitev in the name of Atzei Levonah].

Superficially, it seems clear that this split which is validated in the upper lobe is only on the side of the back, but on the side of the front, a split on the front side is treifah as has been explained, because it is destined to separate; and what does it matter to me if it is other lobes or if it is this lobe, for ultimately it will separate. However, there are great later authorities who validated even on the front side in this lobe [Bach and Panim Me'irot, Noda BiYehudah siman 11] and wrote the reason is because the windpipe holds it so that it does not fall, and they validate even with a cavity beneath it [Noda BiYehudah]. And there are those who wrote that in a place where they validate an extra lobe on the front side, in this case too one should validate, but not in a place where they rule it treifah [Beit Ephraim subsection 60]. And there are those from whose words it is implied that specifically regarding an extra lobe one should validate in this lobe on the front side even in a place where they forbid an extra lobe on the front side, but not regarding a split, and this requires further study in all of this [in the Bach and in the Noda BiYehudah it is explained even regarding a split, and in the Tevuot Shor and Pri Megadim in the Mishbetzot Zahav subsection 8 it is implied regarding an extra lobe, see there].

All these matters were stated only regarding domestic and wild animals, but a bird does not have the division of lobes found in a domestic animal, and if they are found, they have no known number. And similarly regarding kids and tender lambs up to thirty days [Shach, subsection 46], some say that one should not declare it treifah if lobes are not found even without any recognition or slit at all, for such is their growth and their way, that in youth they do not have them, and as they grow, the lobes grow with them. And specifically when they have none at all; but if on one side they have a division of lobes, there must also be on the second side, and if not, it is treifah [ibid. and Taz], for we see that they have already grown, and we do not say that on one side they grew and on the second side they have not yet grown, for presumably both sides grow equally. And there is one who wavers even on the essence of this law [see Pri Chadash]. And similarly the great later authorities wrote that in wild animals and in the wild ox called "bufli," two varda lobes are always found [and it is possible that this is what Rav Huna said to Rav Assi in the Gemara, page 47: all these wild animals have them so; and according to the explanation of our teacher Ephraim in Tosafot there, it refers to two varda lobes].
